author: buchanan_robert
text:
The father had gone out into the night. The cat came back
with meowing, and sat on my knee all alone, And I played softly
on the floor before my candle.
And when I heard him speak, how gently and low!
“My life is just one long tale of loneliness,” said
the cat; “but some day you must tell it.”
It went away again after that, but sometimes at
night it would come back and sit by me and watch
me play and listen to my tales.

text: This is what we would call free verse. The first thing that struck me was how simple it looked on paper! It also reminded me somewhat of haiku because the author uses two lines instead of three. As an aside, it may be possible that this form arose from ancient oral poetry forms (such as proverbs or riddles) which were written down after being passed through generations. Whatever its origins, though, I think there are some similarities between Haiku and Free Verse poems. There are several things about them that make for good writing experiences, such as brevity. text:
‘The old man is so stubborn!’
He gets up from his chair, and looks out
At the sky above the rooftops, where one star shines —
A blue ray on a cold night. He smiles; but soon
His lips are hard as flint again, and no wind
Can turn them or make them bend. He walks along
To call me down from my work beside the fire,
And says, ‘It’ll rain now.’ And then he goes away
Without waiting for an answer. It rains all day.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
O soul, who from thy cradle

Hast been ever mindful
Of him that led thee forth
To tread this vale of tears;

Whose hand so tenderly bore thee through all the ways
That lead to bliss or pain:

Who taught thee first the alphabet of joy and sorrow ;

And bade thee read on every page thou couldst open wide thine eyes,
And mark with heart-felt gratitude each line of praise,
Each word that spoke of His name.
